➡️ Données liées aux services ou utilisateurs
➡️ Éventuels documents sensibles

👉 À ce stade, la nature exacte des données n’a pas été confirmée publiquement.

➡️ Fuite publique de données sensibles

➡️ Atteinte à l’image de marque
➡️ Revente potentielle des données sur des forums

👉 Le message des hackers évoque également la possibilité de causer des “problèmes numériques” supplémentaires, ce qui pourrait inclure des actions de perturbation.

👉 Ce type d’attaque repose sur une stratégie simple : mettre la pression pour obtenir un paiement rapide avant divulgation.

👉 À ce stade, aucune confirmation officielle complète n’a été communiquée par Rockstar Games concernant l’ampleur réelle de l’incident.

👉 Cette affaire illustre une nouvelle fois la montée des attaques de type extorsion + fuite de données, devenues une méthode privilégiée des groupes cybercriminels.

👉 Une situation à suivre de près, alors que les cyberattaques ciblant les grandes entreprises continuent de se multiplier.

Ordigard piraté : des milliers de données médicales exposées

Le site Ordigard, une plateforme utilisée pour la gestion des remplacements dans le secteur médical (notamment entre médecins et étudiants remplaçants), a été victime d’un piratage récemment revendiqué par un hacker.

Selon les informations disponibles, une fuite de données a eu lieu, touchant à la fois des professionnels de santé et des étudiants.

➡️ Données compromises :
🔵 41 médecins : nom, prénom, numéro de téléphone
🔵 4 663 étudiants remplaçants : nom, prénom, numéro de téléphone

Ces informations personnelles, bien que limitées, peuvent être exploitées à des fins de phishing, d’usurpation d’identité ou de démarchage frauduleux.

Pour le moment, on ignore encore l’ampleur exacte de l’attaque et si d’autres données plus sensibles ont été affectées.

👉 Cet incident rappelle une nouvelle fois que même les plateformes spécialisées dans le domaine médical ne sont pas à l’abri des cyberattaques, et souligne l’importance de la sécurisation des données personnelles.

Iliad visé par une revendication de piratage par un groupe de ransomware (5,53 Go)

Le groupe de ransomware ALP-001 revendique le piratage de Iliad, acteur majeur des télécommunications, avec une fuite supposée de données techniques liées aux infrastructures réseau.

Les données proviendraient d’un dataset d’ingénierie réseau mobile couvrant des mesures terrain et des projets télécoms, avec un sample de 5,53 Go partagé comme preuve ; la base complète serait potentiellement bien plus volumineuse et annoncée comme stockée en privé, donc exploitable.

Données compromises :

👉 Mesures radio (RSRP, RSSI, SINR)
👉 Tests GPS (drive tests, coordonnées)
👉 Données de calibration & optimisation réseau
👉 Rapports réglementaires
👉 Données de design réseau
👉 Tests de vitesse et latence
👉 Données 3G / 4G / LTE
👉 Zones et projets spécifiques (villes, déploiements)

breaches.Description: In March 2026, the hacker and extortion group "ShinyHunters" claimed to have obtained a substantial corpus of data from ZenBusiness, a business formation and compliance platform. The group claimed the data had been exfiltrated from platforms including Snowflake, Mixpanel and Salesforce, and threatened to publish it if a ransom was not paid. The following month, after claiming payment had not been made, ShinyHunters publicly released the data. The collection amounted to many terabytes across thousands of files that appeared to originate from multiple systems and business functions, including leads, support records and other CRM-related data. The data contained approximately 5M unique email addresses, often accompanied by name and phone number depending on the source file.

breaches.content: In March 2026, the Colombian fintech company Addi identified unauthorised activity on its platform and advised customers that "it is possible that your personal information may have been compromised". The "pay or leak" extortion group ShinyHunters subsequently claimed responsibility and published a large trove of personal data allegedly obtained from Addi. The data included 34M unique email addresses from credit scoring requests, credit bureau records, customer identity records and email validation logs. It also contained government issued IDs (Cédula de Ciudadanía), estimated income, socioeconomic levels, purchases and other credit-related data points.

breaches.Name: Cerballiance
breaches.Title: Cerballiance
breaches.Description:
Piratage Cerballiance : noms, emails, comptes rendus médicaux et numéros de sécurité sociale exposés

Le secteur de la santé de nouveau ciblé par des hackers. Le réseau de laboratoires Cerballiance, qui suit près de 28 millions de patients par an, informe d’un accès non autorisé à des données personnelles via un prestataire informatique.

Les données concernées incluent notamment nom, prénom, email, mots de passe chiffrés, comptes rendus d’analyses médicales et numéro de sécurité sociale (NIR).

➡️ Incident lié à un prestataire externe
➡️ Données de santé et identifiants exposés (NIR inclus)
➡️ Réseau national touché (millions de patients)
➡️ Risque élevé de phishing / escroqueries ciblées
➡️ Mots de passe réinitialisés, vigilance recommandée
➡️ Aucune exploitation confirmée à ce stade

breaches.Name: Métropole d'Aix-Marseille-Provence
breaches.Title: Métropole d'Aix-Marseille-Provence
breaches.Description:
24/03/26 : La Métropole Aix-Marseille-Provence communique sur une fuite de données

Une fuite liée à un sous-traitant aurait exposé des adresses email d’usagers.

➡️ Risque de divulgation de mots de passe
➡️ Accès temporairement bloqué à certains services
➡️ Recommandation de changer ses mots de passe

La CNIL a été informée de l’incident.
------

Selon les déclarations de l’auteur de l’attaque, la base de données du site ampmetropole.fr aurait été extraite récemment impactant 20000 personnes.
Celle-ci proviendrait d’une instance de développement mal configurée datant de mi-2023, qui aurait été laissée exposée pendant plusieurs années par Inetum.com.
Toujours selon ces affirmations, cette instance serait hébergée sur un domaine enregistré sous l’ancienne appellation du groupe, GFI Informatique (nom abandonné depuis 2020), d’après les informations WHOIS.

Confirmé le 17 mars
Revendiqué le 12 mars
Le secteur de la santé une nouvelle fois ciblé par un piratage.

Medoucine est une plateforme française qui met en relation des patients avec des praticiens en médecines douces (naturopathie, acupuncture, sophrologie, méditation…), avec réservation de consultations en ligne.

➡️ Un acteur revendique sur un forum cybercriminel la vente d’une base contenant 813 866 comptes utilisateurs, dont environ 6 500 praticiens.

➡️ La base inclurait également 70 adresses email gouvernementales (.gouv.fr) selon l’auteur de la revendication.

📊 Données compromises :

👉 nom, prénom
👉 email, numéro de téléphone
👉 historique de réservations / consultations
👉 653 982 emails uniques
👉 804 983 numéros de téléphone

breaches.Title: Le Musée Fabre
breaches.Description:
Le Musée Fabre à Montpellier informe ses visiteurs d’une fuite de données concernant sa billetterie en ligne.

L’incident serait très probablement lié au piratage du prestataire de billetterie Vivaticket, victime d’une attaque par un groupe de ransomware encore inconnu à ce stade.

➡️ Vivaticket est utilisé par plus de 3 500 organisations dans plus de 50 pays et traite près de 850 millions de billets chaque année, ce qui explique l’ampleur potentielle de l’incident.

Les données potentiellement exposées incluent :
👉 adresses email
👉 historique d’achats
👉 nom et prénom
👉 pays / code postal

L’attaque contre Vivaticket pourrait ainsi impacter de nombreux musées, sites culturels et institutions utilisant cette plateforme de billetterie.

breaches.Title: Indigo (stationnement)
breaches.Description:
Un piratage revendiqué par le groupe ransomware Secp0 viserait Indigo Group, l’un des plus grands opérateurs mondiaux de stationnement et parkings urbains (gestion de parkings publics, infrastructures de mobilité et stationnement dans de nombreuses villes).

Selon la publication du groupe, les systèmes auraient été massivement compromis et une base de données très importante aurait été exfiltrée.

➡️ 897 000+ fichiers uniques exposés
➡️ 1 707 433 fichiers au total (avec doublons)
➡️ 27 000+ organisations concernées
➡️ 27 000+ individus identifiés dans les données

📊 Types de données compromises :

👉 327 497 fichiers contenant des informations business confidentielles
👉 360 921 fichiers contenant des données financières
👉 59 624 fichiers contenant des données clients (dont actionnaires)
👉 23 737 fichiers contenant des informations de santé confidentielles

⚠️ Les pirates affirment avoir publié un moteur de recherche dans les données, ainsi qu’un échantillon de la base compromise.

Ameriprise further advised that they have "implemented heightened monitoring of your account(s) to include enhanced identity verification procedures".

breaches.Description:
16/02/26 : Le service public confirme une fuite de données sur la plateforme “Choisir le Service Public”, impactant plus de 377 000 utilisateurs.

--

Un hacker affirme avoir compromis la plateforme officielle « Choisir le service public », portail de recrutement de la fonction publique française.

Selon la publication, les données de 377 418 candidats à des postes du secteur public seraient mises en vente sur un forum de cybercriminalité, suggérant une exposition massive et structurée des informations.

La fuite revendiquée comprend une base complète de profils, avec des données hautement sensibles et directement identifiantes. Un échantillon de lignes a été rendu public pour appuyer la crédibilité de l’attaque.

📂 Données potentiellement compromises :

👉🏻 Identité complète (prénom, nom, civilité, date de naissance)
👉🏻 Coordonnées personnelles (email, téléphone, adresse, code postal, ville, pays)
👉🏻 Niveau d’études et diplômes
👉🏻 Spécialités professionnelles et postes recherchés
👉🏻 Langues parlées et niveaux de maîtrise
👉🏻 Catégories hiérarchiques visées (dont encadrement supérieur)
👉🏻 Métadonnées internes (ID client, dates de création, dernière connexion, durée de rétention)

breaches.Title: IFAPME
breaches.Description:
Un hacker met en vente sur un forum une base de données présentée comme provenant de l’IFAPME.
Pour rappel, l’IFAPME (Institut wallon de Formation en Alternance et des indépendants et PME) est un organisme public belge chargé de la formation des indépendants, entrepreneurs et apprentis en Wallonie.

La base annoncée contiendrait les données de plus de 700 000 personnes ainsi que plus de 85 000 numéros IBAN.

Les extraits partagés montrent des informations personnelles très détaillées et directement exploitables pour des fraudes, du phishing ciblé ou de l’usurpation d’identité.

👉 Noms et prénoms
👉 Adresses postales
👉 Emails
👉 Numéros de téléphone
👉 Dates de naissance
👉 Numéros de registre national
👉 IBAN et informations bancaires
👉 Données administratives liées aux bénéficiaires

Ce type de fuite expose directement les victimes à des arnaques crédibles (faux organismes publics, faux remboursements, escroqueries bancaires, phishing ciblé) et pose de lourds enjeux en matière de protection des données personnelles et de conformité RGPD.

breaches.Description:
Un hacker affirme proposer à la vente une base attribuée à Birdee, service d’investissement en ligne lié à BNP Paribas, fermé depuis juin 2025. Les données analysées semblent crédibles, mais l’authenticité de la fuite reste à confirmer officiellement. Plusieurs milliers de personnes figureraient dans les fichiers.

Dans la majorité des lignes, l’IBAN et le solde ne sont pas renseignés, mais certaines entrées affichent bien des montants investis et, pour quelques profils, des IBAN, ce qui suffit déjà à exposer des personnes à des arnaques financières ciblées.

👉 Nom / prénom
👉 Email
👉 Montants investis (pour certaines entrées)
👉 Date de naissance
👉 Adresse / téléphone
👉 IBAN (présent sur certaines lignes)

Si la fuite se confirme, le risque principal reste le phishing crédible et les tentatives d’escroqueries financières ciblées contre d’anciens clients de la plateforme.

breaches.Name: Ciffreobona
breaches.Title: Ciffreobona
breaches.Description:
Un hacker vient de publier sur un forum une base clients complète issue d’un piratage qui n’aurait jamais été communiqué, concernant Ciffreobona (acteur BTP / fournitures pour pros), avec une fuite qui daterait de 2024 mais qui touche en réalité des clients sur une très longue période (2009 à 2024), pros comme particuliers.

Les données exposées sont suffisamment détaillées pour permettre du phishing ciblé, de l’usurpation d’identité et de la prise de comptes à grande échelle.

Au-delà de la fuite elle-même, le vrai problème est la gestion des données : mots de passe stockés en clair, informations personnelles complètes, aucune protection minimale apparente, ce qui rend l’exploitation immédiate et augmente fortement le risque de compromission en cascade pour les victimes.

Exemple de données exposées dans l’échantillon :
👉🏾 identité, email, téléphone

@biomerieux. L’entreprise est un acteur majeur du diagnostic médical (tests, réactifs, instruments et logiciels utilisés par les laboratoires et hôpitaux dans le monde entier), avec un rôle clé en santé publique.

Les assaillants affirment avoir exfiltré un volume important de données lors de la compromission. L’ampleur exacte et la nature des informations exposées restent à confirmer, mais une attaque de ce type sur un acteur du diagnostic fait peser des risques élevés sur la confidentialité des données internes, les processus opérationnels et, potentiellement, des données liées aux activités de laboratoire.

👉 Éléments techniques / systèmes IT
👉 Potentielles données liées aux opérations de diagnostic

Ce type d’attaque est particulièrement critique pour un acteur de la santé : au-delà du risque de fuite, l’impact opérationnel peut affecter la continuité des services et la chaîne de diagnostic.

breaches.Title: Association Nationale des Premiers Secours (ANPS)
breaches.Description:
Un pirate indique la mise en vente d’une base de données complète présentée comme provenant du site de l’Association Nationale des Premiers Secours (ANPS), organisation qui promeut les gestes de premiers secours et mène des missions de sécurité civile à l’échelle nationale.

Selon les éléments mentionnés dans l’annonce, cette base de données contiendrait des informations issues de systèmes internes de l’association et porterait sur plusieurs milliers d’enregistrements.

Les éléments visibles indiquent la présence de données à caractère personnel et sensibles, incluant notamment des dossiers de victimes, des informations concernant des agents internes, ainsi que des données liées à des interventions médicales.

Les informations compromises mentionnées comprennent également des données personnelles et de contact, telles que des adresses postales, adresses email et numéros de téléphone.

• Dossiers de victimes
• Informations personnelles (identité, coordonnées)
• Données relatives à des interventions médicales
• Adresses email
• Numéros de téléphone
• Informations concernant des agents internes

breaches.Description: In January 2026, the automated investment platform Betterment confirmed it had suffered a data breach attributed to a social engineering attack. As part of the incident, Betterment customers received fraudulent crypto-related messages promising high returns if funds were sent to an attacker-controlled cryptocurrency wallet. The breach exposed 1.4M unique email addresses, along with names and geographic location data. A subset of records also included dates of birth, phone numbers, and physical addresses. In its disclosure notice, Betterment stated that the incident did not provide attackers with access to customer accounts and did not expose passwords or other login credentials.

Plusieurs bases de données attribuées à Fitness Park ont récemment été publiées sur différents forums.

L’analyse des fichiers diffusés indique qu’ils contiennent des informations relatives à des clients et anciens clients de l’enseigne, issues de systèmes internes et associées à de nombreux clubs en France.

Les métadonnées présentes dans les fichiers montrent que de nombreuses lignes datent d’avril 2025, laissant supposer un incident de sécurité survenu à cette période.

Les données exposées incluent des informations personnelles, certaines partiellement masquées, mais relevant néanmoins du champ des données à caractère personnel au sens du RGPD.

👉 À ce jour, et à ma connaissance, Fitness Park n’a jamais communiqué publiquement sur cet incident.

⚠️ Données compromises identifiées dans les fichiers :

• Noms et prénoms
• Dates de naissance
• Sexe
• Statut client (client / ancien client)
• Identifiants internes
• Références club

breaches.Name: SynthientCredentialStuffingThreatData
breaches.Title: Synthient Credential Stuffing Threat Data
breaches.Description: During 2025, the threat-intelligence firm Synthient aggregated 2 billion unique email addresses disclosed in credential-stuffing lists found across multiple malicious internet sources. Comprised of email addresses and passwords from previous data breaches, these lists are used by attackers to compromise other, unrelated accounts of victims who have reused their passwords. The data also included 1.3 billion unique passwords, which are now searchable in Pwned Passwords. Working to turn breached data into awareness, Synthient partnered with HIBP to help victims of cybercrime understand their exposure.

breaches.Name: NotSOCRadar
breaches.Title: Not SOCRadar
breaches.Description: In August 2024, over 332M rows of email addresses were posted to a popular hacking forum. The post alleged the addresses were scraped from cybersecurity firm SOCRadar, however an investigation on their behalf concluded that "the actor merely utilised functionalities inherent in the platform's standard offerings, designed to gather information from publicly available sources". There is no suggestion the incident compromised SOCRadar's security or posed any risk to their customers. In total, the data set contained 282M unique addresses of valid email address format.

breaches.Title: Alleged-SOCRadar
breaches.Description: SOCRadar faced allegations from a threat actor, identified as USDoD, claiming a leak of over 330 million email addresses. However, SOCRadar's investigation revealed no breach of its internal systems. The actor had legitimately acquired access to SOCRadar's platform and utilized its capabilities to gather publicly available email addresses from Telegram channels. SOCRadar confirmed that no customer data or sensitive internal information was compromised.

breaches.Name: LuLu
breaches.Title: LuLu

The impacted data included 190k email addresses and associated phone numbers which were subsequently shared on a popular hacking forum. The following month, the threat of leaking the full database was carried out and a backup from October 2022 with a further 2.6M unique email addresses appeared. This data also included names, physical addresses, orders and PBKDF2 password hashes.

breaches.Description: In June 2024, a huge trove of data from spyware maker mSpy was obtained by hacktivists and published online. The data was predominantly support tickets seeking help to install the spyware on target devices, whilst the attachments contained various data including screen grans of financial transactions, photos of credit cards and nude selfies.

breaches.Name: Spytech
breaches.Title: Spytech
breaches.Description: In July 2024, spyware maker Spytech suffered a data breach that exposed data collected as recently as the previous month. Designed to "invisibly record everything users do", the breach exposed information related to both purchasers and targets of the product. Target data collection (and subsequent exposure) included the infected computer name, browsing history, applications used, usernames of authenticated users, keywords being monitored, file operations (creation and deletion), computer usage times and email addresses, often captured within the spyware's logs. The data also included the names, purchases and md5 password hashes of purchasers.

breaches.Title: The Post Millennial
breaches.Description: In May 2024, the conservative news website The Post Millennial suffered a data breach. The breach resulted in the defacement of the website and links posted to 3 different corpuses of data including hundreds of writers and editors (IP, physical address and email exposed), tens of thousands of subscribers to the site (name, email, username, phone and plain text password exposed), and tens of millions of email addresses from thousands of mailing lists alleged to have been used by The Post Millennial (this has not been independently verified). The mailing lists appear to be sourced from various campaigns not necessarily run by The Post Millennial and contain a variety of different personal attributes including name, phone and physical address (depending on the campaign). The data was subsequently posted to a popular hacking forum and extensively torrented.

breaches.Description: In April 2023, the stolen identity marketplace Genesis Market was shut down by the FBI and a coalition of law enforcement agencies across the globe in "Operation Cookie Monster". The service traded in "browser fingerprints" which enabled criminals to impersonate victims and access their online services. As many of the impacted accounts did not include email addresses, "8M" is merely an approximation intended to indicate scale. Other personal data compromised by the service included names, addresses and credit card information, although not all individuals had each of these fields exposed.

breaches.Name: Eye4Fraud
breaches.Title: Eye4Fraud
breaches.Description: In February 2023, data alleged to have been taken from the fraud protection service Eye4Fraud was listed for sale on a popular hacking forum. Spanning tens of millions of rows with 16M unique email addresses, the data was spread across 147 tables totalling 65GB and included both direct users of the service and what appears to be individuals who'd placed orders on other services that implemented Eye4Fraud to protect their sales. The data included names and bcrypt password hashes for users, and names, phone numbers, physical addresses and partial credit card data (card type and last 4 digits) for orders placed using the service. Eye4Fraud did not respond to multiple attempts to report the incident.

breaches.Name: Duolingo
breaches.Title: Duolingo
breaches.Description: In August 2023, 2.6M records of data scraped from Duolingo were broadly distributed on a popular hacking forum. Obtained by enumerating a vulnerable API, the data had earlier appeared for sale in January 2023 and contained email addresses, names, the languages being learned, XP (experience points), and other data related to learning progress on Duolingo. Whilst some of the data attributes are intentionally public, the ability to map private email addresses to them presents an ongoing risk to user privacy.

breaches.Name: Gemini

breaches.Description: In late 2022, a hacker posted a data set to a public hacking forum which they alleged was sourced from the Gemini crypto exchange, a claim that was later proven to be false as the data was traced back to an incident at a third-party vendor. Twilio described the incident as stemming from a sophisticated social engineering attack designed to steal employee credentials.

In a disclosure notice later shared in August 2022, Twitter advised that the vulnerability was related to a bug introduced in June 2021 and that they are directly notifying impacted customers. breaches.Description: During October 2021, 3.1 million email addresses with accounts on the cryptocurrency market capitalisation website CoinMarketCap were discovered being traded on hacking forums. Whilst the email addresses were found to correlate with CoinMarketCap accounts, it's unclear precisely how they were obtained. CoinMarketCap has provided the following statement on the data: "CoinMarketCap has become aware that batches of data have shown up online purporting to be a list of user accounts. We have not found any evidence of a data leak from our own servers — we are actively investigating this issue and will update our subscribers as soon as we have any new information."

breaches.Name: AllegedATT
breaches.Title: AT&T
breaches.Description: In March 2024, tens of millions of records allegedly breached from AT&T were posted to a popular hacking forum. Dating back to August 2021, the data was originally posted for sale before later being freely released. At the time, AT&T maintained that there had not been a breach of their systems and that the data originated from elsewhere. 12 days later, AT&T acknowledged that data fields specific to them were in the breach and that it was not yet known whether the breach occurred at their end or that of a vendor. AT&T also proceeded to reset customer account passcodes, an indicator that there was sufficient belief passcodes had been compromised. The incident exposed names, email and physical addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers and US social security numbers.

AndroidLista did not respond when contacted about the breach.

Passwords stored as bcrypt hashes were also exposed.

breaches.Name: LinkedInScrape
breaches.Title: LinkedIn Scraped Data (2021)
breaches.Description: During the first half of 2021, LinkedIn was targeted by attackers who scraped data from hundreds of millions of public profiles and later sold them online. Whilst the scraping did not constitute a data breach nor did it access any personal data not intended to be publicly accessible, the data was still monetised and later broadly circulated in hacking circles. The scraped data contains approximately 400M records with 125M unique email addresses, as well as names, geographic locations, genders and job titles. LinkedIn specifically addresses the incident in their post on An update on report of scraped data.

breaches.Title: WeLeakInfo
breaches.Description: In March 2021, the Stripe account of the now-defunct WeLeakInfo service was taken over by "pompompurin" after acquiring an expired domain name with an email address used to manage the account. Only a small number of accounts included email addresses and / or passwords stored as bcrypt hashes with a total of 66.5k unique email addresses being exposed across the corpus of data.

Impacted data also included email addresses, the country logged in from and the date and time each login occurred alongside device information including the make and model, IMSI number and serial number.

Many records within the data also included additional personal attributes such as names, phone numbers, IP addresses, dates of birth and genders. No passwords were included in the data. The Verifications.io website went offline during the disclosure process, although an archived copy remains viewable.

breaches.Name: GoldSilver
breaches.Title: GoldSilver
breaches.Description: In October 2018, the bullion education and dealer services site GoldSilver suffered a data breach that exposed 243k unique email addresses spanning customers and mailing list subscribers. An extensive amount of personal information on customers was obtained including names, addresses, phone numbers, purchases and passwords and answers to security questions stored as MD5 hashes. In a small number of cases, passport, social security numbers and partial credit card data was also exposed. The data breach and source code belonging to GoldSilver was publicly posted on a dark web service where it remained months later. When notified about the incident, GoldSilver advised that "all affected customers have been directly notified".

The data was discovered by security researcher Vinny Troia who subsequently sent a subset of the data containing 126 million unique email addresses to Have I Been Pwned. The data left exposed by Apollo was used in their "revenue acceleration platform" and included personal information such as names and email addresses as well as professional information including places of employment, the roles people hold and where they're located. The Apollo website has a contact form for those looking to get in touch with the organisation.

Read more about spam lists in HIBP.

breaches.Name: 8tracks
breaches.Title: 8tracks
breaches.Description: In June 2017, the online playlists service known as 8Tracks suffered a data breach which impacted 18 million accounts. In their disclosure, 8Tracks advised that "the vector for the attack was an employee’s GitHub account, which was not secured using two-factor authentication". Salted SHA-1 password hashes for users who didn't sign up with either Google or Facebook authentication were also included. The data was provided to HIBP by whitehat security researcher and data analyst Adam Davies and contained almost 8 million unique email addresses. The complete set of 18M records was later provided by JimScott.Sec@protonmail.com and updated in HIBP accordingly.

breaches.Name: Bell2017
breaches.Title: Bell (2017 breach)
breaches.Description: In May 2017, the Bell telecommunications company in Canada suffered a data breach resulting in the exposure of millions of customer records. The data was consequently leaked online with a message from the attacker stating that they were "releasing a significant portion of Bell.ca's data due to the fact that they have failed to cooperate with us" and included a threat to leak more. The impacted data included over 2 million unique email addresses and 153k survey results dating back to 2011 and 2012. There were also 162 Bell employee records with more comprehensive personal data including names, phone numbers and plain text "passcodes". Bell suffered another breach in 2014 which exposed 40k records.

breaches.Name: MasterDeeds
breaches.Title: Master Deeds
breaches.Description: In March 2017, a 27GB database backup file named "Master Deeds" was sent to HIBP by a supporter of the project. Upon detailed analysis later that year, the file was found to contain the personal data of tens of millions of living and deceased South African residents. The data included extensive personal attributes such as names, addresses, ethnicities, genders, birth dates, government issued personal identification numbers and 2.2 million email addresses. At the time of publishing, it's alleged the data was sourced from Dracore Data Sciences (Dracore is yet to publicly confirm or deny the data was sourced from their systems). On 18 October 2017, the file was found to have been published to a publicly accessible web server where it was located at the root of an IP address with directory listing enabled. The file was dated 8 April 2015.

The impacted data classes far exceeds those listed for the breach and differ between the thousands of impacted sites.

An archive of the data was subsequently shared on a popular hacking forum in May 2020 and redistributed broadly.

breaches.Name: AntiPublic
breaches.Title: Anti Public Combo List
breaches.Description: In December 2016, a huge list of email address and password pairs appeared in a "combo list" referred to as "Anti Public". The list contained 458 million unique email addresses, many with multiple different passwords hacked from various online systems. The list was broadly circulated and used for "credential stuffing", that is attackers employ it in an attempt to identify other online systems where the account owner had reused their password. For detailed background on this incident, read Password reuse, credential stuffing and another billion records in Have I Been Pwned.

The hack of the vBulletin forum led to the exposure of over 366k accounts along with email and IP addresses, dates of birth and salted passwords hashed with MD5. The owner of the MrExcel forum subsequently self-submitted the data to HIBP.

breaches.Name: Rankwatch
breaches.Title: RankWatch
breaches.Description: In approximately November 2016, the search engine optimisation management company RankWatch exposed a Mongo DB with no password publicly whereupon their data was exfiltrated and posted to an online forum. The data contained 7.4 million unique email addresses along with names, employers, phone numbers and job titles in a table called "us_emails". When contacted and advised of the incident, RankWatch would not reveal the purpose of the data, where it had been acquired from and whether the data owners had consented to its collection. The forum which originally posted the data explained it as being "in the same vein as the modbsolutions leak", a large list of corporate data allegedly used for spam purposes.

The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com.

breaches.Name: AdultFriendFinder2016
breaches.Title: Adult FriendFinder (2016)
breaches.Description: In October 2016, the adult entertainment company Friend Finder Networks suffered a massive data breach. The incident impacted multiple separate online assets owned by the company, the largest of which was the Adult FriendFinder website alleged to be "the world's largest sex & swinger community". Exposed data included usernames, passwords stored as SHA-1 hashes and 170 million unique email addresses. This incident is separate to the 2015 data breach Adult FriendFinder also suffered. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com.

breaches.Name: ExploitIn
breaches.Title: Exploit.In
breaches.Description: In late 2016, a huge list of email address and password pairs appeared in a "combo list" referred to as "Exploit.In". The list contained 593 million unique email addresses, many with multiple different passwords hacked from various online systems. The list was broadly circulated and used for "credential stuffing", that is attackers employ it in an attempt to identify other online systems where the account owner had reused their password. For detailed background on this incident, read Password reuse, credential stuffing and another billion records in Have I Been Pwned.

breaches.Name: ModernBusinessSolutions
breaches.Title: Modern Business Solutions
breaches.Description: In October 2016, a large Mongo DB file containing tens of millions of accounts was shared publicly on Twitter (the file has since been removed). The database contained over 58M unique email addresses along with IP addresses, names, home addresses, genders, job titles, dates of birth and phone numbers. The data was subsequently attributed to "Modern Business Solutions", a company that provides data storage and database hosting solutions. They've yet to acknowledge the incident or explain how they came to be in possession of the data.

breaches.Name: JustDate
breaches.Title: Justdate.com
breaches.Description: An alleged breach of the dating website Justdate.com began circulating in approximately September 2016. Comprised of over 24 million records, the data contained various personal attributes such as email addresses, dates of birth and physical locations. However, upon verification with HIBP subscribers, only a fraction of the data was found to be accurate and no account owners recalled using the Justdate.com service. This breach has consequently been flagged as fabricated; it's highly unlikely the data was sourced from Justdate.com.

breaches.Title: Leet
breaches.Description: In August 2016, the service for creating and running Pocket Minecraft edition servers known as Leet was reported as having suffered a data breach that impacted 6 million subscribers. The incident reported by Softpedia had allegedly taken place earlier in the year, although the data set sent to HIBP was dated as recently as early September but contained only 2 million subscribers. The data included usernames, email and IP addresses and SHA512 hashes. A further 3 million accounts were obtained and added to HIBP several days after the initial data was loaded bringing the total to over 5 million.

breaches.Title: eThekwini Municipality
breaches.Description: In September 2016, the new eThekwini eServices website in South Africa was launched with a number of security holes that lead to the leak of over 98k residents' personal information and utility bills across 82k unique email addresses. Emails were sent prior to launch containing passwords in plain text and the site allowed anyone to download utility bills without sufficient authentication. Various methods of customer data enumeration was possible and phishing attacks began appearing the day after launch.

Real Estate Mogul was advised of the incident in September 2018 and stated that they "found no instance of user account credentials like usernames and passwords nor billing information within this file".

breaches.Name: Digimon
breaches.Title: Digimon
breaches.Description: In September 2016, over 16GB of logs from a service indicated to be digimon.co.in were obtained, most likely from an unprotected Mongo DB instance. The service ceased running shortly afterwards and no information remains about the precise nature of it. Based on enquiries made via Twitter, it appears to have been a mail service possibly based on PowerMTA and used for delivering spam. The logs contained information including 7.7M unique email recipients (names and addresses), mail server IP addresses, email subjects and tracking information including mail opens and clicks.

The leaked data was extensive and included names, physical, email and IP addresses, genders and birth dates, account balances and passwords stored as plain text.

breaches.Name: MDPI
breaches.Title: MDPI
breaches.Description: In August 2016, the Swiss scholarly open access publisher known as MDPI had 17.5GB of data obtained from an unprotected Mongo DB instance. The data contained email exchanges between MDPI and their authors and reviewers which included 845k unique email addresses. MDPI have confirmed that the system has since been protected and that no data of a sensitive nature was impacted. As such, they concluded that notification to their subscribers was not necessary due to the fact that all their authors and reviewers are available online on their website.

The data in the breach contains usernames, email addresses and salted MD5 password hashes and was provided to HIBP by white hat security researcher and data analyst Adam Davies. Read more about Chinese data breaches in Have I Been Pwned.

breaches.Name: Snapchat
breaches.Title: Snapchat
breaches.Description: In January 2014 just one week after Gibson Security detailed vulnerabilities in the service, Snapchat had 4.6 million usernames and phone number exposed. The attack involved brute force enumeration of a large number of phone numbers against the Snapchat API in what appears to be a response to Snapchat's assertion that such an attack was "theoretical". Consequently, the breach enabled individual usernames (which are often used across other services) to be resolved to phone numbers which users usually wish to keep private.
